content: Cerebral palsy (CP) is a group of non-progressive disorders affecting posture and movement, caused by damage to the developing brain. Children with CP, particularly those with limited gross motor function, are at a higher risk of developing osteoporosis, which increases their likelihood of fractures. The severity of gross motor function in children with CP is classified using the Gross Motor Function Classification System (GMFCS). Bisphosphonates are medications known to increase bone mineral density (BMD) and reduce fracture rates, and they are widely used in the treatment of osteoporosis in adults. However, their use in children with CP remains controversial due to limited evidence and a lack of recent clinical trials evaluating their efficacy and safety in this population. The objective of this review was to assess the efficacy and safety of bisphosphonate therapy for treating low BMD or secondary osteoporosis in children with CP (GMFCS Levels III to V) under the age of 18. A comprehensive search was conducted in September 2020 across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and Embase, as well as trial registries. Reference lists of relevant studies were also reviewed, and authors of identified studies were contacted to locate unpublished data. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs that compared bisphosphonates (administered orally or intravenously at any dose) to placebo or no treatment in children with CP and low BMD or osteoporosis. Standard Cochrane methodologies were used for data collection and analysis. However, due to insufficient data, meta-analyses could not be performed, and the results were presented narratively. Two RCTs involving a total of 34 participants were identified. Both studies included children with non-ambulatory CP or CP with osteoporosis. The participants in these studies were similar in terms of CP severity, age, and sex distribution. The trials used different bisphosphonate medications and intervention durations, but further comparisons were limited due to insufficient published data from one of the trials. One trial received funding from research and hospital foundations, with pharmaceutical companies providing components of calcium and vitamin supplements, while the other trial did not disclose its funding sources. One study was judged to have a high risk of bias, and the other had an unclear risk of bias. For the primary outcome, both studies provided very low-certainty evidence suggesting that bisphosphonate treatment may improve BMD at least four months after the intervention. Only one study, involving 12 participants, provided sufficient detail to assess the effect size, reporting an improvement in lumbar spine z-scores six months post-intervention (mean difference of 18%, 95% confidence interval 6.57 to 29.43; very low-certainty evidence). Regarding secondary outcomes, one study provided very low-certainty evidence that bisphosphonate reduced serum N-telopeptides (NTX) more effectively than placebo. Another study reported that both bisphosphonate combined with alfacalcidol and alfacalcidol alone reduced NTX levels, but no direct comparison between the groups was made. For serum bone-specific alkaline phosphatase (BAP), one study reported inconclusive results between groups, while the other study found reductions in BAP with both bisphosphonate plus alfacalcidol and alfacalcidol alone, again without comparing the groups. Neither study reported data on changes in volumetric BMD in the distal radius or tibia, fracture frequency, bone pain, or quality of life. One study noted febrile events in two participants during the initial dosing schedule, but no other adverse events were reported in either study. In conclusion, the available evidence provides very low certainty that bisphosphonate treatment may improve bone health in children with CP. Only one study with 14 participants contributed to the assessment of effect size, resulting in low precision of the effect estimate. Furthermore, only one planned primary outcome could be evaluated due to insufficient reporting in the studies. Additional RCTs are needed to better understand the efficacy and safety of bisphosphonates in this population. Future research should also address optimal standard treatments, including weight-bearing exercises, vitamin D, and calcium supplementation, and should prioritize fracture frequency as a primary outcome.
